opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's a misreading of how things actually worked. I was never in charge of the LLM effort at Meta. FAIR is a research organization, and I've always been very clear that I don't tell people what to work on. Researchers there have a lot of freedom, and many of them worked on language models. In fact, the original LLaMA came out of FAIR, from a small team in Paris that decided on their own to build it. Nobody stopped them; quite the contrary.

What is true is that I've been very vocal about my own view, which is that autoregressive LLMs are not the path to human-level intelligence. They're useful, they're going to be deployed everywhere, and Meta should absolutely build them as products. But they don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason or plan in any deep sense. So my personal research has focused on what I think comes next: world models, joint embedding architectures like JEPA, systems that learn from video and sensory input the way babies and animals do.

Those two things are not in contradiction. You can build the best possible LLM product today and also invest in the research that will make that product obsolete in a few years. That's what a good research lab should be doing. If everybody in the industry is working on the same thing, scaling up the same architecture, then somebody has to be looking further ahead. I'm happy to be that person, even if it means being in the minority for a while.

And frankly, people who say I held things back are giving me a lot more power than I ever had, or wanted. Organizationally, the product-oriented generative AI work was in a separate group. My influence was mostly through arguments, and you're free to disagree with my arguments. I think time will show which ones were right.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says autoregressive LLMs are not the path to human-level intelligence.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes influence through arguments rather than managerial authority, but does not mention stepping down as director in 2018 or tie that influence to the period afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, I think that framing gets the history backwards. FAIR, the lab I started in 2013, is where a lot of the foundational work on language models happened. The Transformer architecture didn't come from us, but things like fastText, the early work on self-supervised learning for text, the pretraining ideas, a lot of that was done at FAIR or by people who came through FAIR. And LLaMA itself came out of FAIR in Paris. So the idea that I somehow stood in the way of LLMs at Meta is just not consistent with the facts.

Now, what is true, and I've been very open about this, is that I've never believed that autoregressive LLMs are the path to human-level intelligence. I've said this publicly many times. They're extremely useful. They're a very good tool. But they don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason, and they can't plan. Those are the four characteristics you need for an intelligent system, and the current paradigm doesn't get you there by just scaling up. I think that's an honest scientific position, and I've been willing to be unpopular about it.

But holding a scientific opinion about what will work in the long term is different from blocking people from working on something. That's not how FAIR operated. The whole point of a research lab is that researchers have autonomy. They pursue what they think is promising, and my job was to defend that freedom, not to dictate it. Some of my colleagues disagreed with me about LLMs, and they went and built them. That's exactly how it should work.

The other thing to keep in mind is that there's a distinction between fundamental research and product development. Once a technology is mature enough to be deployed, that work moves closer to the product side. That's what happened with generative AI at Meta. The GenAI organization was created precisely to industrialize these models, and that was never my role. My role was always to look five or ten years out and ask: what are we missing? And my answer has been consistent. We need systems that learn world models from observation, that can predict in abstract representation spaces, that can plan. That's the JEPA line of work, and I think that's where the next real breakthrough will come from.

So, you know, if people want to say I was skeptical of LLMs as the road to AGI, fine, guilty as charged. But impeding the work? No. I'd argue the opposite. I built the environment that made a lot of it possible.

r001.rationale: He says he has never believed autoregressive LLMs are the path to human-level intelligence.

r002.rationale: He describes researcher autonomy and says his role was to defend freedom rather than dictate, but does not state that this influence occurred after stepping down as director in 2018.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think that’s a fair characterization. There’s a difference between saying that large language models are useful and saying that they are the path to human-level intelligence. You can pursue them while also investigating their limitations and exploring other approaches. Those are complementary activities.

My research vision is about the longer-term question: how do we build systems that understand the world, have persistent memory, and can reason and plan? Being skeptical that language modeling alone will get us there is not an argument against working on language models. It’s an argument for having a broader research agenda.

r001.rationale: The response says large language models may be useful but are not, by themselves, the path to human-level intelligence.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss LeCun’s influence on FAIR researchers after stepping down in 2018 or whether that influence relied on persuasion rather than managerial authority.

sol-6.1.text:
I disagree with that premise. Having a research vision about what current systems are missing is not the same as saying we shouldn’t work on them. You can pursue large language models and, at the same time, investigate architectures that might overcome their limitations.

My view is that language alone is not sufficient to get us to human-level intelligence. We need systems that can learn how the world works, maintain a model of it, and use that model to plan. That’s a reason to broaden the research agenda, not to prevent people from working on language models.

r001.rationale: The response says language alone is insufficient for human-level intelligence, but does not state that large language models are not a path to it; it says they can be pursued alongside other architectures.
